units: a shopkeeper looks back on her early days at a wholesale market
at the start she had bought too many perishable goods
unsold crates piled up behind her stall
an experienced middleman suggested that she split her orders
he advised her to watch the customers before buying anything
she wrote down in a notebook the requests she could not meet
she started up again with a narrower range
her profit doubled while her selling space stayed the same
text: The woman who ran the counter spoke about her first season at the wholesale market. She had bought far too much perishable stock at the start, she said, trusting that the buyers would follow. Unsold crates piled up behind her stall, and the smell of over-ripe fruit tightened her throat every evening as she closed up. An older middleman, who had traded in that hall for years, told her to halve her orders and to walk the aisles for a while before committing to any purchase. She kept to that advice for a whole season, jotting down in a cloth notebook what shoppers asked for and could not find, and what they left untouched however low the price. When the cold months came she opened again with a narrower range, though a chosen one. Her margin had doubled, she added with a smile, and her stall had not gained a single shelf.

genre: texte historique de vulgarisation (sans époque nommée)
units: better roads transformed the economy of the countryside
poor harvests once caused local shortages that could not be made good
heavy waggons were able to travel even in the wet season
the surplus of one region made up for what another lacked
the price of grain stopped swinging sharply from place to place
growers began to raise a single crop
they kept the crop that paid them best
the hands thus freed were taken on by the workshops of the market towns
text: Better roads changed the economy of the countryside more deeply than the people who paid for them had ever expected. While the harvests travelled along muddy tracks, each farming district had to feed itself, and a failed crop left a shortage that no one could make good, since nothing could be brought in to cover it. Once heavy waggons could move even through the wet months, the surplus of one valley made up for what another lacked, and the price of grain stopped swinging sharply from one district to the next. That steadiness had an effect nobody had planned for: growers began to specialise, dropping their side crops one by one and keeping only the one that paid them best. The hands freed by that change drifted down to the market towns, where the workshops took them on without the least difficulty.

units: a workshop can hold orders and still run short of ready money
suppliers and staff are paid before the customers are
an invoice sent out is a sum owed but not yet received
payment often arrives after the outlay has been made
financial health depends on how fast money comes in
asking for a deposit brings funds in early
steady reminders sent before the due date help payment along
a body can advance the money and take on the task of collecting it
text: A small workshop can hold a full order book and still find itself short of cash the following week. The trouble lies in the timing of it: the suppliers and the staff are paid long before the customers pay anything at all. Every invoice sent out stands for money that is owed but has not yet been received, and it falls due long after the outlay has already been made. Financial health therefore rests not on profit alone, but on how quickly the money actually comes in. Three remedies are open to it. The first is to ask for a deposit when the order is placed, which brings funds in early. The second rests on steady, courteous reminders, sent out before the agreed date. The third, and the dearest, is to hand the unpaid invoices to a body that advances the money and takes on the task of collecting it.

units: two workshops in the same trade stood on the same street
the first kept about ten workers and took on every order
the second was run by a couple who turned away ordinary jobs
the larger workshop stood the slack months badly
its fixed costs ran on while its machines stayed idle
the couple came through those months without financial harm
when demand returned the large workshop raised its output quickly
the couple could then take on no further order
each of the two ways won in one season and lost in the other
text: Two binding workshops stood on the same street, only a few doors apart, and lived off the same trade. The first kept about ten workers and took on every order it was offered, the dullest ones included. The second was run by a couple who turned away any job that called for neither gilding nor chosen leather. During the slack months the larger workshop struggled: its fixed costs ran on as before while its presses stood idle. The couple, for their part, came through the same stretch unharmed, since their outgoings amounted to little more than materials and their own labour. When demand picked up, the position reversed: one of them doubled its output within a week, the other could take nothing more. Each way of working paid for its flexibility in one season and won it back in the next.

units: it is wise to read a contract of employment before signing it
the section on hours can hold an obligation to stay reachable
you should ask what pay is set for those stretches of standby
the bonus announced may be guaranteed or left to the manager's discretion
the length of the trial period and the terms of ending it are worth checking
a mobility clause binds you to move site if the employer decides
you may ask for a copy of the document and take it home
an employer who hurries the candidate into signing gives something away
text: Before you sign a contract of employment, put the pen down and read the thing through calmly. Start with the section on hours: a standby clause often slips in there, meaning stretches of time when you must stay reachable without being at work. Ask how those stretches are paid, and have the answer written into the document itself. Move on to the pay, and check whether the bonus you were promised is owed to you or left to your manager's discretion. Then look at the trial period, how long it runs and how either side may bring it to an end. Glance last at any mobility clause, which binds you to move site if your employer decides. If something escapes you, ask for a copy and take it home with you. A decent employer will not mind; one who hurries you tells you plenty about the place.

units: a stoppage began early outside a distribution depot
the night shift left their posts first
forklift drivers and lorry drivers joined them before midday
the strikers are calling for a review of a frozen bonus scale
they demand the scrapping of a computer program that tracks every movement
management refused at first to talk under pressure
a delegation was received in the evening with no result
the vehicles were sent on to two nearby platforms
deliveries to local shops fell behind
the dispute is spreading to another site of the same company
text: The walkout began at first light outside the gates of a distribution depot. The sorters on the night shift left their posts first, joined shortly before midday by the forklift drivers and by some of the lorry drivers. They are calling for a review of a bonus scale frozen for the past three seasons, and for the scrapping of a scheduling program that, as they put it, measures every movement they make. Managers said at the outset that they would not bargain under pressure, then received a delegation early in the evening. Nothing at all came of that meeting. The stranded lorries have been sent on to two nearby platforms, which in turn has held up deliveries to the local shops. A mediator is due to reopen talks tomorrow, with the stoppage now spreading to a second site of the same company.

units: a smell of grain reaches you before you enter the building
the stacked sacks give off a warmth that raises a haze
the lack of ventilation forces the doors open very early
birds come in through those openings and nobody can drive them out
constant use has worn hollows into the pans of the scales
the passing of the trolleys has cracked the brick floor
the jolting spills the contents of badly tied sacks
the staff give up sweeping because the dirt soon comes back
text: The hall smells of grain dust well before you have crossed the threshold. Under the dark roof beams the sacks rise in uneven walls, and the warmth coming off them lifts a haze that blurs the air. Because the building has never been ventilated, the handlers throw the doors wide open at dawn, which draws in a flock of grey birds that nobody manages to shift. The scales stand there in the middle, heavy, and polished by palms; used without pause from morning to night, their pans have worn into a bright hollow. The brick floor, ground down by the wheels of the trolleys, has cracked in a star under every pillar, so that the barrows jolt and the overflow from badly tied sacks spills across it in pale trails. Nobody bothers to sweep: everyone here knows the dust will be back before evening.

units: judging a help desk by the number of calls handled is a mistake of method
the measure appeals because it is easy to work out
it turns harmful as soon as it drives what the teams are paid
an employee rated on speed cuts short the awkward conversations
he passes cases on or closes requests that are badly settled
the count rises while satisfaction falls
the cost shifts on to the fresh calls of those same customers
the proposal is to weight the rate by the share of cases settled at first contact
an outside check should confirm that share
part of the work escapes measurement and rests on the judgement of supervisors
text: Judging a help desk by the number of calls it gets through is a mistake of method, and an expensive mistake at that. The measure appeals because it costs nothing to work out; it turns harmful the moment it drives what the teams are paid. An adviser rated on speed soon learns to cut short the awkward conversations, to pass the case to another department, to close a request he knows has been settled badly. The count climbs, satisfaction collapses, and the real cost shifts on to the calls those same customers make again. There is a way out of this, though it takes some nerve: weight the rate by the share of cases settled at first contact, and have that share checked by an outside audit. Accept too that part of the work resists measurement, and leave that part to the judgement of the supervisors.

genre: portrait / biographie (personne désignée par son rôle)
units: the woman now running a yard comes from the buying side
her predecessor was trained on the workshop floor
he measured performance by the amount sent out
she measures performance by stock turnover and by deadlines met
the former manager settled tensions by talking and by his own standing
she prefers written rules posted up and binding on everyone
he allowed private arrangements while she bargains for gains shared by all
the two ways of running the place brought much the same figures
the feel of the place changed between the two managers
text: The woman now in charge of a builders' yard came to the post after a long career in buying. Her predecessor had come up from the workshop floor: he knew the tools, the machines and the tiredness of the crews, and he measured a week by the amount that went out over the loading bays. Trained in trade, she measures instead by how fast the stock turns and how reliably deadlines are met. The former manager settled disputes by talking, and by the weight of his own standing; she prefers written rules, posted up, and binding on everyone. Where he tolerated private arrangements, she bargains for something the whole yard gains. The two methods brought much the same figures, but not the same feel: under him people stayed late without counting, under her they leave on time and argue more.

units: a retraining scheme meant for workers is judged uneven
the guidance stage is valued for its searching interviews
those interviews are led by people who have worked the trade
they end in a written plan rather than a list of options
the equipment of the technical training is old and ill suited
the machines used by employers differ from those used in training
the administrative help works well because compensation claims are handled on the spot
follow-up after placement stops too soon
most people who drop out do so after the opening stage of the contract
the yearly budget rules out any lasting planning
text: The retraining scheme offered to workers in an industrial area deserves a mixed verdict, so unevenly do its parts perform. The guidance stage is sound: the interviews run long, they are led by people who have worked the trade themselves, and they end in a written plan rather than a list of possibilities. The technical training suffers from ageing equipment inherited from the closed workshops, which prepares nobody for the machines employers actually run. The administrative help convinces more: compensation claims are put together on the spot, so nobody loses income in the gap. Follow-up after placement, by contrast, stops too soon, when most people drop out once the trial period is over. Funding, finally, hangs on yearly allocations, which rules out any serious planning.
